draft.title: Designing better fuel cells
card: Green chemistry is a set of principles for designing products and processes that cut waste and hazards. Chemists use it to guide changes to fuel cell design.

a fuel cell is more efficient when more of the fuel's chemical energy becomes electrical energy and less is lost as heat. Better catalysts at the electrodes help by speeding up the electrode reactions.

designers aim to use materials that are less toxic and less harmful to mine, use and dispose of. Some fuel cells use expensive platinum catalysts, so one aim is to use less platinum or replace it with more common materials.
A better design also has to meet society's energy needs. It should supply enough power, last a long time and use fuel that is produced in a way that does not create large amounts of waste.
draft.remember: Better fuel cells waste less energy and use safer materials, while still meeting society's need for power.

a.q: A team develops a catalyst that lets a fuel cell convert more fuel energy into electricity and lose less as heat. Which green chemistry aim does this meet?
opts: Greater energy efficiency
Use of safer materials
Lower cost of the fuel
A higher cell voltage from the fuel
a.why: Turning more of the fuel's chemical energy into electrical energy and losing less as heat is greater energy efficiency. It is not about safer materials, because nothing in the case changes how hazardous the materials are.
a.clue: Think about where the energy goes: electricity or heat.

b.q: Dana's company makes a fuel cell that uses a cheap, non-toxic metal catalyst in place of platinum, with the same power output. Which is the best reason this is a green chemistry improvement?
opts: It uses safer, more common materials without losing power
It makes the fuel cell run without any fuel at all
It stops the fuel cell producing any waste heat
It raises the energy stored in each unit of fuel
b.why: Swapping platinum for a cheap, non-toxic catalyst is a safer materials change, and the same power output means society's needs are still met. The fuel cell still needs fuel, and nothing in the case says heat loss or the energy in the fuel changed.
b.clue: Look at what changed in the case: the catalyst material, not the fuel or the heat.

b.best: It uses safer, more common materials without losing power

problems.detail: Two distractors are implausible ('run without any fuel at all', 'stops ... any waste heat'), and the card already says fuel cells need fuel and lose some heat. A Year 12 student can rule them out without knowing the idea, so the question is too easy.

The 'Safer materials' bullet gives cost as the reason for replacing platinum ('expensive platinum catalysts'). Platinum is not notably toxic, so this mixes cost with safety and could suggest that cheaper means safer. The reason should be framed as the hazard and impact of mining a scarce metal, or cost should be kept separate.

check.summary: Both keyed answers are correct and the facts check out. Question b's distractors are too implausible to test understanding, and the card blurs cost with safety when it explains replacing platinum.

proposal.title: Designing better fuel cells
card: Green chemistry is a set of principles for designing products and processes that cut waste and hazards. Chemists use it to guide changes to fuel cell design.

a fuel cell is more efficient when more of the fuel's chemical energy becomes electrical energy and less is lost as heat. Better catalysts at the electrodes help by speeding up the electrode reactions.

designers aim to use materials that are less toxic and less harmful to mine, use and dispose of. Platinum catalysts rely on a scarce metal whose mining disturbs land and uses a lot of energy, so one aim is to use less platinum or replace it with more abundant materials. Cost is a separate issue: a cheaper material is not automatically a safer one.
A better design also has to meet society's energy needs. It should supply enough power, last a long time and use fuel that is produced in a way that does not create large amounts of waste.
proposal.remember: Better fuel cells waste less energy and use safer materials, while still meeting society's need for power.

a.q: A team develops a catalyst that lets a fuel cell convert more fuel energy into electricity and lose less as heat. Which green chemistry aim does this meet?
opts: Greater energy efficiency
Use of safer materials
Use of a less hazardous fuel
A longer working life for the cell
a.why: Turning more of the fuel's chemical energy into electrical energy and losing less as heat is greater energy efficiency. It is not about safer materials, because nothing in the case changes how hazardous the materials are.
a.clue: Think about where the energy goes: electricity or heat.

b.q: Dana's company replaces the platinum catalyst in its fuel cell with an abundant, non-toxic metal. The cell gives the same power from the same amount of fuel. Why is this a green chemistry improvement?
opts: It uses safer, more abundant materials and keeps its power
It turns more of the fuel's energy into electricity
It uses a fuel that is produced with less waste
It costs less, and a cheaper material is a safer one
b.why: Swapping scarce platinum for an abundant, non-toxic metal is a safer materials change, and keeping the same power means society's needs are still met. It is not an efficiency gain, because the same fuel gives the same power. Lower cost does not by itself make a material safer.
b.clue: The fuel and the power output stayed the same. What did change?

b.best: It uses safer, more abundant materials and keeps its power
